# pigz - Parallel Implementation of GZip

pigz (pronounced "pig-zee") is a parallel implementation of gzip that compresses files using multiple processors and cores.

## What pigz does

pigz is a fully functional replacement for gzip that exploits multiple processors and multiple cores to compress data faster. It can compress and decompress files in gzip, zlib, and zip formats.

## Basic Usage

```
pigz [options] [files...]
unpigz [options] [files...]
```

If no files are specified or "-" is given as a filename, pigz reads from standard input.

## Key Features

- **Parallel compression**: Splits input into chunks (default 128 KB) and compresses them in parallel
- **Multiple output formats**: Supports gzip, zlib, and single-entry zip formats
- **Compatible with gzip**: Can decompress any gzip file; gzip can decompress any pigz-compressed file
- **Independent blocks**: Optional mode for partial error recovery and random access
- **rsyncable**: Optional mode for rsync-friendly output

## Common Options

- **-#** (1-9, 11): Set compression level (1=fastest, 9=best, 11=zopfli for maximum compression)
- **-d, --decompress**: Decompress files
- **-k, --keep**: Keep original files (don't delete after compression)
- **-c, --stdout**: Write output to stdout
- **-p n**: Use n processors (default: all available)
- **-b n**: Set block size to n KB (default: 128)
- **-i, --independent**: Compress blocks independently
- **-R, --rsyncable**: Make output rsync-friendly
- **-l, --list**: List contents of compressed files
- **-t, --test**: Test integrity of compressed files
- **-f, --force**: Force overwrite of output files
- **-r, --recursive**: Recursively compress directories
- **-z, --zlib**: Use zlib format instead of gzip
- **-K, --zip**: Use zip format (single entry)
- **-v, --verbose**: Verbose output
- **-h, --help**: Display help

## Examples

Compress a file using all available processors:
```
pigz file.txt
```

Compress with maximum compression (slower):
```
pigz -11 file.txt
```

Decompress a file:
```
pigz -d file.txt.gz
# or
unpigz file.txt.gz
```

Compress to stdout:
```
pigz -c file.txt > file.txt.gz
```

Compress with 4 processors and keep the original:
```
pigz -k -p 4 file.txt
```

Test compressed file integrity:
```
pigz -t file.txt.gz
```

## Environment Variables

- **GZIP**: Options read from this variable before command line options
- **PIGZ**: Options read from this variable after GZIP but before command line options

## File Formats

pigz produces standard gzip, zlib, or zip format output. Any tool that can decompress these formats can decompress pigz output, and pigz can decompress any standard gzip file.

## Performance

The input is broken into chunks that are compressed in parallel. Each chunk is compressed independently with the last 32K of the previous chunk used as a dictionary to maintain compression effectiveness. The number of threads defaults to the number of available processors.

Decompression uses a single thread for the actual decompression, but creates additional threads for reading, writing, and checksum calculation.

## More Information

For complete documentation, see the pigz man page (pigz.1 or pigz.pdf).

## Author

pigz was written by Mark Adler.

.SH SYNOPSIS

.RB [ " \-cdfhikKlLmMnNqrRtz0..9,11 " ]
[
.B -b
.I blocksize
]
[

.I threads
]
[

]
[

]

[

]

.SH DESCRIPTION
.I Pigz
compresses using threads to make use of multiple processors and cores.
The input is broken up into 128 KB chunks with each compressed in parallel.
The individual check value for each chunk is also calculated in parallel.
The compressed data is written in order to the output, and a combined check
value is calculated from the individual check values.
.PP
The compressed data format generated is in the gzip, zlib, or single-entry
zip format using the deflate compression method.  The compression produces
partial raw deflate streams which are concatenated by a single write thread
and wrapped with the appropriate header and trailer, where the trailer
contains the combined check value.
.PP
Each partial raw deflate stream is terminated by an empty stored block
(using the Z_SYNC_FLUSH option of zlib), in order to end that partial bit
stream at a byte boundary.  That allows the partial streams to be
concatenated simply as sequences of bytes.  This adds a very small four to
five byte overhead to the output for each input chunk.
.PP
The default input block size is 128K, but can be changed with the
.B -b
option.  The number of compress threads is set by default to the number
of online processors,
which can be changed using the
.B -p
option.  Specifying
.B -p 1
avoids the use of threads entirely.
.PP
The input blocks, while compressed independently, have the last 32K of the
previous block loaded as a preset dictionary to preserve the compression
effectiveness of deflating in a single thread.  This can be turned off using
the
.B -i
or
.B --independent
option, so that the blocks can be decompressed
independently for partial error recovery or for random access. This also
inserts an extra empty block to flag independent blocks by prefacing
each with the nine-byte sequence (in hex): 00 00 FF FF 00 00 00 FF FF.
.PP
Decompression can't be parallelized, at least not without specially prepared
deflate streams for that purpose.  As a result,
.I pigz
uses a single thread
(the main thread) for decompression, but will create three other threads for
reading, writing, and check calculation, which can speed up decompression
under some circumstances.  Parallel decompression can be turned off by
specifying one process
(
.B -dp 1
or
.B -tp 1
).

If no names are provided on the command line, or if "-" is given as a name (but
not after "--"), then the input is taken from stdin. If the GZIP or PIGZ

.B \-6.

.TP

.TP

# The pigz zip format is quite specific. Let me analyze the format carefully:
# Local header:
# PK\x03\x04 - signature
# 2d 00 - version needed: 45 (ZIP64)
# 08 00 - general purpose bit flag: bit 3 set (data descriptor)
# 08 00 - compression method: 8 (deflate)
# 4d 73 - DOS time
# 9d 5c - DOS date  
# 00 00 00 00 - CRC (0, in data descriptor)
# ff ff ff ff - compressed size (ZIP64 marker)
# ff ff ff ff - uncompressed size (ZIP64 marker)
# 01 00 - filename length: 1
# 1d 00 - extra field length: 29 bytes
# 2d - filename "-"
# 01 00 - extra field tag? No...
# Let me decode more carefully

python3 -c "
data = bytes.fromhex('504b03042d000800080049739d5c0000000000000000ffffffffffffffff0100' + '1d00' + '2d' + '0110000000000000000000000000000000000000000055540500010000000000')
# local header:
print('sig:', data[0:4].hex())
print('ver needed:', int.from_bytes(data[4:6], 'little'))
print('flags:', hex(int.from_bytes(data[6:8], 'little')))
print('method:', int.from_bytes(data[8:10], 'little'))
print('dos time:', int.from_bytes(data[10:12], 'little'))
print('dos date:', int.from_bytes(data[12:14], 'little'))
print('crc32:', int.from_bytes(data[14:18], 'little'))
print('comp size:', int.from_bytes(data[18:22], 'little'))
print('uncomp size:', int.from_bytes(data[22:26], 'little'))
print('name len:', int.from_bytes(data[26:28], 'little'))
print('extra len:', int.from_bytes(data[28:30], 'little'))
print('name:', data[30:31])
print('extra:', data[31:31+29].hex())
"

# Now I understand the ZIP format used. Let me analyze it:
# - Local header: uses ZIP64 with fake comp/uncomp sizes (0xFFFFFFFF)
# - Data descriptor uses ZIP64 (8-byte) sizes
# - Central directory: has real sizes, no ZIP64 extension in CD extra
# - End of central dir: regular (not ZIP64)
# - Version made by in CD: 0xff2d (strange - probably 0x032d = Unix/45)

# Let me check the version made by more carefully
python3 -c "
vmb = 0xff2d
print(f'Version made by: {vmb}')
print(f'  OS: {vmb >> 8}')  # 255 = ?
print(f'  Version: {vmb & 0xff}')  # 45
# Actually in ZIP spec: byte 0 = version (45), byte 1 = OS
# OS 255 is unusual... let me check
# Actually the bytes are: 2d ff => little-endian => 0xff2d
# byte 0 of version-made-by = 0x2d = 45 (version)
# byte 1 = 0xff = 255 (OS type)
# Or maybe it's actually treated differently
print(f'bytes: {vmb.to_bytes(2, little_endian=True)}')
" 2>/dev/null || python3 -c "
vmb = 0xff2d
print(f'Version made by: {vmb}')
print(f'  OS: {(vmb >> 8) & 0xff}')
print(f'  Version: {vmb & 0xff}')
print(f'bytes LE:', vmb.to_bytes(2, byteorder='little'))
"

# Actually let me check which suffixes are accepted:

    cp /tmp/test_t.gz /tmp/sfx_test$sfx 2>/dev/null
    result=$(./executable -d -c /tmp/sfx_test$sfx 2>&1)
    if echo "$result" | grep -q "does not have compressed suffix"; then
        echo "NOT accepted: $sfx"
    elif echo "$result" | grep -q "unrecognized format"; then
        echo "Format error (accepted suffix): $sfx"
    else
        echo "Accepted: $sfx"
    fi
done

# This is because: when -S is specified, pigz uses the suffix for COMPRESSION

# UNLESS we're writing to stdout (-c), in which case it strips any suffix

# Actually wait - let me re-read the manual:
# "-S --suffix .sss: Use suffix .sss instead of .gz (for compression)"
# So -S only applies to compression suffix, not decompression

# For decompression: always use the builtin suffix list
# The suffixes are: .gz, .zz, .zip, .tgz, .Z (not .taz, .bz2, etc.)

# Let me verify .Z handling:
cp /tmp/test_t.gz /tmp/zdot.Z
./executable -dk /tmp/zdot.Z 2>&1
ls /tmp/zdot* 2>/dev/null

# Mine: 04 (level=0 uses "fastest" flag? But level 0 = no compression)
# Original: 00 (no flag for level 0)

# My code: if(g_level<=1)xfl=4; else if(g_level>=9)xfl=2;
# For level 0: 0 <= 1 is TRUE, so xfl=4. That's wrong!
# The original uses xfl=0 for level 0.
# Level 0 should map to xfl=0 (since it's no compression, not "fastest" compression)
# Fix: only set xfl=4 for level==1, not for level<=1

python3 << 'EOF'
with open('pigz.c','r') as f: code=f.read()
old = 'unsigned char xfl=0;if(g_level<=1)xfl=4;else if(g_level>=9)xfl=2;'
new = 'unsigned char xfl=0;if(g_level==1)xfl=4;else if(g_level>=9)xfl=2;'
print('Found:', old in code)
code=code.replace(old,new)
with open('pigz.c','w') as f: f.write(code)
print('Done')
EOF
gcc -O2 -o my_pigz pigz.c -lz -lpthread -lm 2>&1 | grep error
echo "hello" | ./my_pigz -c -0 | od -A x -t x1z
echo "hello" | ./executable -c -0 | od -A x -t x1z

        break

# When stdin is a regular file (redirected), original gets the FILE'S mtime!
# Mine gets 0. This is a significant difference.

# Original pigz behavior:
# 1. When stdin is a regular file: use its mtime in gzip header
# 2. When stdin is a pipe/terminal: use mtime=0

# I need to detect if stdin is a regular file and get its mtime.
# Use fstat(STDIN_FILENO, &st) to check if it's a regular file.

python3 << 'EOF'
with open('pigz.c','r') as f: code=f.read()

# Modify do_compress to accept mtime=0 and in the stdin case, get mtime from fstat
# Actually the issue is: for stdin mode, the caller passes mtime=0
# But if stdin is a regular file, we should get mtime from fstat(0)

# Find the do_stdin function and modify it to pass mtime:
old = """    /* compress stdin to stdout */
    do_compress(stdin,stdout,NULL,0);"""

new = """    /* compress stdin to stdout */
    /* if stdin is a regular file, use its mtime */
    time_t stdin_mt=0;
    struct stat stdin_st;
    if(fstat(0,&stdin_st)==0&&S_ISREG(stdin_st.st_mode))stdin_mt=stdin_st.st_mtime;
    do_compress(stdin,stdout,NULL,stdin_mt);"""

print('Found:', old in code)
code=code.replace(old,new)
with open('pigz.c','w') as f: f.write(code)
print('Done')
EOF
gcc -O2 -o my_pigz pigz.c -lz -lpthread -lm 2>&1 | grep error
./executable -c -p1 -b128 < /tmp/test2b2.bin | od -A x -t x1 | head -1

# - non-independent blocks: strip 5 bytes (the full sync-flush terminator)
# - independent blocks: strip 4 bytes (leave the byte before '00 00 ff ff')

# The idea is that for independent blocks, the deflate stream needs to be cleanly
# byte-terminated (the extra byte makes it properly byte-aligned).

print('For non-independent: strip 5 bytes from non-last blocks')
print('For independent: strip 4 bytes from non-last blocks')

cat /tmp/big.bin | md5sum

    if diff /tmp/rt_test.txt /tmp/rt_test.decomp > /dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo "PASS"
    else
        echo "FAIL"
    fi
done

input.command:
# Let me now look at one remaining issue: the rsync mode.
# I should implement basic rsync support to match the original more closely.
# The rsync mode uses a rolling hash to find block boundaries.

# From the pigz documentation: "Input-determined block locations for rsync"
# The implementation uses a checksum of the last 32 bytes of the uncompressed data.
# When the checksum hits a specific threshold, a new block starts.

# Let me check what the threshold is by examining the behavior:
# With 2MB random data and rsync mode, we got 2 extra sync points (from earlier test).
# That means roughly 2 splits per 2MB = 1 split per 1MB on average for random data.
